name: Size, Sum, Max, Min, Find In Bst
html:
Welcome back, dear reader. So, we hope you are doing well. Let's discuss this problem called SIZE SUM MAX MIN AND FIND IN BST. Well, before we move forward, we want to tell you that you are doing really well up till here. Keep up the hard work. and you will definitely succeed in your motives.

Problem Explanation:

We are given a binary search tree and we have to find its size, sum, max and min and we also have to write the code for the find function. We request you to solve these problems for a Binary Tree first. If you have not solved these problems for a binary tree then you won't be able to understand them here properly.
You may refer to the question video if you have any doubts regarding the question. We request you try to solve this problem yourself first and then refer to the solution to understand the concepts in a better way.

Approach:

Some methods are based only on the physical structure of the tree and do not have anything to do with the data of the tree. Since the binary tree and BST differ only in the terms of the arrangement of data inside the tree, they are completely same as far as physical structure is concerned. Therefore, the functions like size and sum, which depend only on traversing every node of a tree will remain the same as traversing every node of the tree is the same for both binary trees and BST.

  1. Size(): As already discussed above, the size function will remain the same as that we studied in the binary trees. So to sum up quickly, we have a faith that recursion will give us the number of nodes in both the left as well as the right subtrees of a BST. (see fig-1)

    2. So, the size of the tree can be calculated by adding the size of both the sub-trees and adding 1 to it.
    You may refer to the SIZE, SUM, MAX AND HEIGHT OF A BINARY TREE solution video to understand the code for it in detail. The code for this function is given with the code of all the other functions in a later section.

    Watch video
  2. Sum: The sum function also has to traverse all the nodes to get the value of every node and add it to the total sum. So, it is also the same as the sum function that we did for the BST. You may refer to the SIZE, SUM, MAX AND HEIGHT OF A BINARY TREE solution video (1:46-2:42) and (8:06-9:16) to understand the process in detail. The code for the same is given with all the other functions code in a later section of this article. The diagram below shows the recursion faith that we have used to get the sum.
  3. Max: Have a look at the diagram given below:

    4. If we have a tree as shown above and we have to find the maximum value for it then we know that the max value cannot be found in the left sub-tree as it contains smaller values than the root node. So, if there is a value which is greater than the root node then it will be found only in the right subtree. What if there was no right subtree for this tree? Then the root node would have been the max value.
    The max value of a BST is the right-most value in the tree. So, to find the max value, we just have to keep going to the right child until we reach a node who does not have a right child. That node will be the maximum value. (see fig-4). The code for max is given with all the other functions at the last.

  4. Min: Have a look at the diagram given below:

    5. If we have a tree as shown above and we have to find the minimum value for it then we know that the min value cannot be found in the right subtree as it contains greater values than the root node. So, if there is a value which is less than the root node then it will be found only in the left sub-tree. What if there was no left sub-tree for this tree? Then the root node would have been the min value.
    The min value of a BST is the left-most value in the tree. So, to find the min value, we just have to keep going to the left child until we reach a node who does not have a left child. That node will be the minimum value. (see fig-6). The code for the min function is given with all the other functions at the end.

  5. Find: In the binary tree, we traverse through all the nodes of the tree to find a particular value. Here, we will not traverse all the nodes. We can in a way say that here, recursion knows where to travel. Let us take an example tree and try to find a value in it

    6. Have a look at fig-7. We try to find the value 70 in this tree. So, what do you think we should do?

    We compare the input value i.e. 70 with the root value. Since the root value is smaller than the given value, this means that we are looking for a value which is on the right side of the root node. This is simple, right?
    So, if the node value is less than the input value, we get to the right child of the root. (see fig-8)

    Now we are at node (75). This value is greater than the input. So, the value we are looking for i.e. 70 will be present in the left subtree of this node if it is present in the tree.
    So, if the node value is greater than the input value, we go to the left child of the node. (see fig-9)

    Now the node value is smaller than the input value. So, the input value will be in the right subtree of this node. So, we move to its right child.

    Now the node value is equal to the data we were searching for. So, we will return true when node data is equal to the input value.
    Let us say that this value was not 70. So, the value here could have either been greater than 70 or less than 70. If it would have been greater than 70, we would have gone to the left child of this leaf node and we would have reached null. If the value in the leaf node would have been smaller than 70, we would have gone to the right child of this leaf node which is null. So, in both the cases we reach null. This means the value is not found because there was no other position in the tree where the value could have been.
    So, if node=null, then return false.This is the find function. If you have any doubts regarding this, you may refer to the solution video (2:04-2:55) to understand the above procedure.

    Watch video

    Now that we have understood all the methods, let's write the code for all of them.

import java.io.*; import java.util.*; public class Main { public static class Node { int data; Node left; Node right; Node(int data, Node left, Node right) { this.data = data; this.left = left; this.right = right; } } public static class Pair { Node node; int state; Pair(Node node, int state) { this.node = node; this.state = state; } } public static Node construct(Integer[] arr) { Node root = new Node(arr[0], null, null); Pair rtp = new Pair(root, 1); Stack< Pair> st = new Stack<>(); st.push(rtp); int idx = 0; while (st.size() > 0) { Pair top = st.peek(); if (top.state == 1) { idx++; if (arr[idx] != null) { top.node.left = new Node(arr[idx], null, null); Pair lp = new Pair(top.node.left, 1); st.push(lp); } else { top.node.left = null; } top.state++; } else if (top.state == 2) { idx++; if (arr[idx] != null) { top.node.right = new Node(arr[idx], null, null); Pair rp = new Pair(top.node.right, 1); st.push(rp); } else { top.node.right = null; } top.state++; } else { st.pop(); } } return root; } public static void display(Node node) { if (node == null) { return; } String str = ""; str += node.left == null ? "." : node.left.data + ""; str += " <- " + node.data + " -> "; str += node.right == null ? "." : node.right.data + ""; System.out.println(str); display(node.left); display(node.right); } public static int size(Node node) { if (node == null) { return 0; } int ls = size(node.left); int rs = size(node.right); int ts = ls + rs + 1; return ts; } public static int sum(Node node) { if (node == null) { return 0; } int ls = sum(node.left); int rs = sum(node.right); int ts = ls + rs + node.data; return ts; } public static int max(Node node) { if(node.right == null){ return node.data; } else { return max(node.right); } } public static int min(Node node) { if(node.left == null){ return node.data; } else { return min(node.left); } } public static boolean find(Node node, int data){ if(node == null){ return false; } if(data > node.data){ return find(node.right, data); } else if(data < node.data){ return find(node.left, data); } else { return true; } } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { BufferedReader br = new BufferedReader(new InputStreamReader(System.in)); int n = Integer.parseInt(br.readLine()); Integer[] arr = new Integer[n]; String[] values = br.readLine().split(" "); for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) { if (values[i].equals("n") == false) { arr[i] = Integer.parseInt(values[i]); } else { arr[i] = null; } } int data = Integer.parseInt(br.readLine()); Node root = construct(arr); int size = size(root); int sum = sum(root); int max = max(root); int min = min(root); boolean found = find(root, data); System.out.println(size); System.out.println(sum); System.out.println(max); System.out.println(min); System.out.println(found); } }
java; true";

Hope that you have understood all the methods completely. If you have any doubts, you may refer to the complete solution video to clear them. Now let us discuss the time and space complexities of all these methods.

Analysis: Time Complexity: O(n)

Size(): The time complexity of this method is O(n) as we have traversed all the nodes to count them.

Sum(): The time complexity of this method is O(n) as we have traversed all the nodes to add their values into the size.

Max(): The time complexity of this function is O(log2n) as we are not traversing the complete tree. We are at-most traversing the height of the tree which is O(log2n). This is the average case scenario.. If the tree has all the nodes only on the left side (left-skewed) or only on the right side (right-skewed) then the height will become O(n) and the time complexity will also be O(n).

Min(): Same as above for max.

Find(): The time complexity of find is also O(log2n). This is also the average case complexity. It may reach O(n) in the worst case if the tree is left skewed or right skewed.

Space Complexity: O(h)

The space complexity for all these methods will be O(1) without considering the recursion space and O(h) where h is the max height of the recursion stack which is the same as the height of the tree if we consider the recursion space. This h is O(log2n) in an average case scenario but in the worst case scenario it can also be O(n).

So, dear reader, did you understand the time and space complexity analysis too? We hope you did. Try to think of a mathematical proof for these time complexities and the space complexities. With this, we have finished this problem.

Suggestions: O(h)

Our only suggestion for this problem is that you should study these problems for binary trees again and then find the difference between BST and binary tree approaches. Also try to find out some mathematical proof for the time and space complexities. Does this problem tell you why BST is called a binary search tree? Think about this!!! Till then, Happy Coding!!!!
